content.overview: Section 17 lists documents that must be registered, including gifts of immovable property, non-testamentary instruments creating or extinguishing rights of Rs 100 or more in immovable property, and leases from year to year or for more than one year.
content.study: Compulsory registration is the gateway rule. Pair it with section 49 (effect of non-registration) and with TPA formalities such as sale and lease. An unregistered document caught by section 17 generally cannot affect the property or prove the transaction, subject to the section 49 proviso.

learningObjectives: Explain Registration Act, 1908 Section 17 and its role in the registration scheme.
Apply the section to a factual document without confusing compulsory and optional registration.
Connect the provision with related statutory consequences where applicable.
enhancement.definition: Section 17 identifies documents for which registration is compulsory under the Registration Act, 1908, including specified gifts of immovable property, specified non-testamentary instruments affecting rights in immovable property, and specified leases.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: A document falling within a compulsory-registration category must satisfy the statutory registration requirement; the consequences of non-registration are principally addressed by Section 49.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Registration Act, 1908, Section 17(1) and relevant clauses; the exact scope can also be affected by applicable State amendments, which must be checked separately.
essentialIngredients: Identify the nature of the document.
Determine whether it falls within a category expressly covered by Section 17.
For instruments concerning immovable property, identify the right/title/interest affected and the statutory threshold or other trigger.
Check relevant exceptions, exemptions and applicable State amendments.
If compulsory registration applies, consider the consequences under Section 49.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 17 is a classification provision. The analysis should begin with the document and transaction, then match it to the statutory categories rather than assuming that every document concerning immovable property requires registration. For example, the Act specifically addresses gifts of immovable property and specified non-testamentary instruments affecting rights in immovable property. Leases are separately addressed by their duration or rent characteristics. A complete answer should also connect Section 17 to Section 49 because compulsory registration has consequences when the requirement is not satisfied.
examples: A non-testamentary instrument that purports to create a qualifying right or interest in immovable property must first be tested against Section 17; if the provision applies, the document is compulsorily registrable and Section 49 becomes relevant if it is left unregistered.
enhancement.distinctions: Section 17 creates the compulsory-registration rule; Section 18 identifies categories that may be registered; Section 49 states the principal statutory consequences of non-registration.

caseLaw.name: Shakeel Ahmed v. Syed Akhlaq Hussain
caseLaw.holding: The Supreme Court referred to Sections 17 and 49 and held that compulsory registration requirements arise from the statute and that unregistered documents falling within the requirement cannot confer title to immovable property.
caseLaw.relevance: Directly discusses Sections 17 and 49 in the context of unregistered documents affecting immovable property.

enhancement.problemApplication: A parties execute an instrument affecting an interest in immovable property and dispute whether registration is mandatory. Identify the document, the right or interest affected, the applicable Section 17 category, any exception or State amendment, and then apply Section 49 if registration was required.

State the governing rule and ingredients
